full_judgment:
"Disobedience of, or resistance to, a void mandate, order, judgment, or decree, or one issued by a Court without jurisdiction of the subject matter and parties litigant, is not contempt, and where the Court has no jurisdiction to make the order, no waiver can cut off the rights of the party to attack its validity." 

 25. Therefore, in that view of the matter it appears to us that while exercising contempt jurisdiction this Court is competent to examine the legality and validity of the order complained of because this Court working under the Constitution and having the obligation to defend, preserve and protect the Constitution cannot enforce an order or action which appears to be unconstitutional besides being void. The celebrated decision of Marbury vs Madison, 2 LEd 60 is an authority for this, though no authority is really required. Definitely it is the power, nay the duty, of this Court to see that the directions for the compliance of which petition has been made are constitutionally valid directions and this power cannot be denied to this Court on the analogy of an executing Court. Though contempt jurisdiction is availed of to enforce a writ of mandamus, this Court exercising jurisdiction under Article 108 cannot be equated with an executing court. Even an executing court will not execute a void decree or order and the Indian Supreme Court in Nai Babu vs Lala Ramnarayan, AIR 1978 SC 22, observed; 

 "It is true that a decree for eviction of a tenant cannot be passed solely on the basis of a compromise between the parties. The Court is to be satisfied whether a statutory ground for eviction has been pleaded which the tenant has admitted by the compromise. Thus dispensing with further proof, on account of the compromise, the court is to be satisfied about compliance with the statutory requirement on the totality of facts of a particular case bearing in mind the entire circumstances from the stage when the compromise is effected". 

 26. When a compromise decree is challenged as a nullity in the course of its execution the executing court can examine relevant materials to find out whether statutory grounds for eviction existed in law. If the pleadings and other materials on the record make out a prima facie case about the existence of statutory grounds for eviction a compromise decree cannot be held to be invalid and the executing court will have to give effect to it."
